analysis.investment_thesis: Blue Dart is India's premium express logistics brand and a fine company — but at 44x trailing P/E with net profit declining for three consecutive years (382→371→301→252 Cr, FY2022 to FY2025), this is a stalwart being priced like a fast grower, which is one of the most dangerous combinations in investing. The PEG ratio is effectively incalculable in a favorable direction — net profit CAGR over 9 years is just 2.8%.
key_strengths: Dominant premium express logistics brand with 6 Boeing freighters, nationwide network, and DHL backing — genuine moat in the premium courier segment
5/5 positive OCF years with consistent free cash flow (488 Cr in FY2025) — the business reliably converts revenue to cash
Revenue growing at 9.3% CAGR with expanding volume as e-commerce drives India's logistics sector — sector tailwind is real
key_risks: Net profit declining in absolute terms for three consecutive years (FY2022 peak 382 Cr → FY2025 252 Cr, -34%) at a P/E of 44x — this is the wrong direction at the wrong valuation
EBITDA trend is contracting despite revenue growth, pointing to structural margin compression from competition (Delhivery, DTDC, FedEx) and rising fuel/lease costs
PEG ratio of 15.7 (44x P/E / 2.8% profit CAGR) — there is no growth story to justify this multiple
red_flags: Three consecutive years of absolute net profit decline — the business is not just decelerating, it is shrinking in profitability
Debt remains elevated at ~1,008 Cr (largely lease liabilities) while profits contract — financial headroom is tightening
Forward P/E of 27.96 implies a sharp profit recovery in the next 12 months — if that doesn't arrive, the stock has significant downside
analysis.detailed_analysis: Blue Dart is what I call a stalwart — a steady, recognizable business with a real moat. Stalwarts are worth owning at 12-15x earnings for modest appreciation. At 44x trailing P/E with profits heading in the wrong direction, the market is making a classic mistake: paying growth-company multiples for a mature-franchise business. The EBITDA contracting trend despite 9% revenue growth tells you margins are being squeezed by labor, fuel, and competitive pricing. DHL's 75% ownership provides strategic support but also limits upside optionality. I'd revisit this at 20-25x P/E if profits stabilize — right now the math simply doesn't work.
